questions.title: Arteries forming Little's area
questions.question: Little's area is a known spot on the anteroinferior nasal septum that is vulnerable to bleeding because it is an anastomotic network of branches of several arteries. All of the following arteries contribute to it EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The septal branch of the superior labial artery (from the facial artery) is one of the four vessels that anastomose in Little's area, so it does contribute.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The greater palatine artery is a genuine contributor to the Kiesselbach anastomosis and therefore is not the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Little's (Kiesselbach's) area is the anastomosis of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries. There is no artery called the "nasolabial artery" contributing to it — the term is not part of the plexus. It is therefore the odd one out among the listed vessels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery is a major contributor to Little's area, so it is not the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal artery supplies the anterosuperior septum and is one of the four vessels of the Kiesselbach plexus.

questions.subtopic: Little's area and nasal blood supply
questions.learning_objective: List the four arteries that anastomose in Little's (Kiesselbach's) area.

questions.title: Artery that does not share in Little's area
questions.question: Which of the following arteries does NOT share in the anastomosis at Little's area?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal artery is one of the four contributors to Little's area, supplying its anterosuperior part.
explanations.B: Correct. Little's area is formed by the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries. The posterior ethmoidal artery supplies the posterosuperior part of the nasal cavity, not the anteroinferior septum, so it does not participate in the Kiesselbach plexus. It is the correct answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The septal branch of the superior labial artery is a genuine contributor to Little's area.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The greater palatine artery reaches the anterior septum through the incisive canal and shares in the anastomosis.

questions.subtopic: Little's area and nasal blood supply
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the posterior ethmoidal artery does not contribute to Little's area.

questions.title: Spread of nasal vestibule furunculosis
questions.question: Furunculosis of the vestibule of the nose is dangerous because infection may spread to:

explanations.A: Correct. The nasal vestibule lies in the "dangerous area of the face", which drains through the facial and angular veins into the ophthalmic veins and then the cavernous sinus. Because these veins are valveless, infection from a vestibular furuncle can ascend retrogradely and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis. This is why such furuncles must not be squeezed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ethmoid sinus is not the feared route of spread; the danger from a vestibular furuncle is intracranial venous spread to the cavernous sinus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral (sigmoid) sinus is related to spread from ear and mastoid infection, not from a nasal vestibule furuncle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior sagittal sinus is not the characteristic pathway of spread from the nasal vestibule.

questions.subtopic: Nasal vestibule furuncle and the dangerous area of the face
questions.learning_objective: State that a nasal vestibule furuncle can spread to the cavernous sinus.

questions.title: Origin of the anterior ethmoidal artery
questions.question: The anterior ethmoidal artery arises from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The external carotid supplies most of the nose through the maxillary and facial arteries, but not the ethmoidal vessels.
explanations.B: Correct. The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, which itself arises from the internal carotid artery. This is why the ethmoidal supply to the nose comes from the internal carotid system, unlike the sphenopalatine and greater palatine arteries. It also explains why anterior ethmoidal bleeding may need ligation near the orbit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The maxillary artery gives the sphenopalatine and greater palatine arteries, not the anterior ethmoidal artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The facial artery gives the superior labial (septal) branch, not the anterior ethmoidal artery.

questions.subtopic: Little's area and nasal blood supply
questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior ethmoidal artery arises from the internal carotid (ophthalmic) artery.

questions.title: Danger of nasal furunculosis
questions.question: Furunculosis of the nose is dangerous because infection may spread to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spread to the nasal cartilage would cause local chondritis but is not the life-threatening danger that makes a nasal furuncle important.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orbital involvement can occur but the classical feared complication is intracranial venous spread to the cavernous sinus.
explanations.C: Correct. The nose lies within the dangerous area of the face, whose valveless facial and ophthalmic veins connect to the cavernous sinus. Infection from a nasal furuncle can therefore ascend to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, a potentially fatal complication. For this reason nasal furuncles must never be squeezed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sphenoid sinus is not the characteristic route of dangerous spread from a nasal furuncle.

questions.subtopic: Nasal vestibule furuncle and the dangerous area of the face
questions.learning_objective: State that a nasal furuncle can spread to the cavernous sinus.

questions.title: Site of Little's area
questions.question: Little's area is located on the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior turbinate lies on the lateral nasal wall and is not the site of Little's area.
explanations.B: Correct. Little's area is a small region on the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum. It is the site of the Kiesselbach arterial anastomosis and the commonest source of anterior epistaxis. Its exposed, superficial vessels make it prone to bleeding from trauma or drying.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The middle meatus is on the lateral wall and receives sinus drainage; it is not Little's area.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sphenoethmoidal recess is the posterosuperior drainage area of the sphenoid sinus, not the site of Little's area.

questions.subtopic: Little's area and nasal blood supply
questions.learning_objective: State that Little's area is on the anteroinferior nasal septum.

questions.title: Vessels of the Kiesselbach plexus
questions.question: The Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area is formed by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Labial branch of the facial artery
options.B: Septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. The septal (superior labial) branch of the facial artery is one of the four vessels of the Kiesselbach plexus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery is a major contributor to the plexus.
explanations.C: Correct. The Kiesselbach plexus is formed by the superior labial (facial), sphenopalatine, greater palatine and anterior ethmoidal arteries. The pharyngeal (ascending pharyngeal) artery supplies the nasopharynx and does not reach Little's area. It is therefore the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior ethmoidal artery contributes the anterosuperior part of the plexus.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The greater palatine artery reaches the anterior septum and shares in the plexus.

questions.subtopic: Little's area and nasal blood supply
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the pharyngeal artery is not part of the Kiesselbach plexus.

questions.title: First treatment of bilateral choanal atresia
questions.question: Bilateral choanal atresia in a neonate is best FIRST treated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transnasal puncture is part of definitive repair, not the immediate life-saving first step in a distressed neonate.
explanations.B: Correct. Neonates are obligate nasal breathers, so bilateral choanal atresia presents as a neonatal airway emergency with cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying. The immediate first measure is to establish an oral airway (an oral airway or a McGovern nipple) to bypass the blocked nose. Definitive surgical repair is carried out later once the airway is secured.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transpalatal repair is a definitive operation performed after the airway has first been secured.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transnasal endoscopic repair is the definitive surgical treatment, not the first emergency step.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that bilateral choanal atresia is first managed by an oral airway before repair.

questions.title: Timing of nasal fracture reduction with oedema
questions.question: Reduction of a nasal bone fracture associated with oedema should be done:

options.C: After one week, so the oedema will subside

explanations.A: Incorrect. When there is marked oedema, immediate reduction is difficult because swelling hides the true position of the nasal bones.
explanations.B: Incorrect. One hour is not long enough for significant oedema to settle.
explanations.C: Correct. When a nasal fracture is masked by oedema, reduction is delayed for about a week until the swelling subsides so that the deformity can be assessed accurately. It must still be done before about two to three weeks, after which the bones unite and reduction is no longer possible. This gives a window of roughly one to two weeks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A displaced nasal fracture should be reduced; leaving it produces a permanent deformity.

questions.learning_objective: State that a nasal fracture with oedema is reduced after about a week once swelling subsides.

questions.title: Unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a child
questions.question: A 4-year-old child presents with a unilateral offensive purulent nasal discharge. The most likely diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. CSF rhinorrhoea is a clear watery discharge, not an offensive purulent one, and is not typical of a young child.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An antrochoanal polyp causes unilateral obstruction but not the classic foul purulent discharge of a retained foreign body.
explanations.C: Correct. A unilateral, offensive, purulent nasal discharge in a young child is a nasal foreign body until proven otherwise. Children commonly insert objects into one nostril, and the retained object produces a foul unilateral discharge. Examination and removal of the foreign body are required.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis produces bilateral watery discharge with sneezing, not a unilateral offensive one.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a child as a nasal foreign body.

questions.title: Management of suspected CSF rhinorrhoea
questions.question: A 20-year-old woman presents with a right unilateral watery nasal discharge that is exaggerated on leaning forward. Management of her condition includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.B: MRI scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biochemical analysis of the fluid (glucose, and specifically beta-2 transferrin) confirms that the discharge is CSF, so it is part of management.
explanations.B: Incorrect. MRI helps show the site and any meningoencephalocele, so it is a legitimate investigation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CT cisternography with intrathecal contrast localises the site of the leak and is a key investigation.
explanations.D: Correct. The picture is CSF rhinorrhoea. Its management is confirmation (biochemistry), localisation (CT cisternography/MRI), conservative measures and, if needed, repair, together with cover against meningitis. Nasal vasoconstrictor (decongestant) drops have no role in CSF rhinorrhoea, so they are the exception.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Systemic antibiotic cover is commonly given to reduce the risk of ascending meningitis while a CSF leak persists, so it is part of management.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that vasoconstrictor drops have no role in the management of CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.title: Key investigation in CSF rhinorrhoea
questions.question: In CSF rhinorrhoea, the most important investigation is:

options.B: Plain X-ray of the paranasal sinuses
options.C: CT cisternography with intrathecal metrizamide, to detect the site of the leak

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiography and embolization are used for vascular lesions and epistaxis, not to localise a CSF leak.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plain sinus X-ray cannot demonstrate the site of a dural defect.
explanations.C: Correct. The crucial step in CSF rhinorrhoea is to localise the site of the dural/bony defect so it can be repaired. CT cisternography with intrathecal contrast (metrizamide) shows the leak point and any associated skull-base defect. High-resolution CT and MRI complement it, but pinpointing the site is what guides surgery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ultrasonography has no role in imaging a skull-base CSF leak.

questions.learning_objective: State that CT cisternography localises the leak in CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.title: Nasal discharge after upper molar extraction
questions.question: After extraction of an upper left molar tooth, a patient has an offensive left nasal discharge and left nasal regurgitation of food and fluid. The diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Correct. The roots of the upper molars are closely related to the floor of the maxillary sinus, so their extraction can open a communication between the mouth and the antrum. The result is an oroantral fistula, presenting with an offensive nasal discharge and regurgitation of food and fluid into the nose on the same side. The temporal link to a molar extraction is characteristic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A malignant nasal tumour is not the expected sequel of a tooth extraction and would present differently.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inverted papilloma causes unilateral obstruction and bleeding, not post-extraction food regurgitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fungal sinusitis is not the classic consequence of a molar extraction with oronasal regurgitation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise offensive nasal discharge with food regurgitation after molar extraction as an oroantral fistula.

questions.title: Nasal fracture reduction without oedema (within a week)
questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents 30 minutes after a blow to his face. There is bleeding from the nose and the nose is deviated to the left, with no obvious facial oedema or ecchymosis. X-ray shows a fractured nasal bone. Reduction of this fracture should be performed:

explanations.A: Correct. When a displaced nasal fracture is seen early and there is no significant oedema, it can be reduced without delay, and in any case within about a week. Reduction must be completed before roughly two to three weeks, after which the nasal bones set and can no longer be moved. Among the options offered, only "within a week" falls inside this window.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By three weeks the nasal bones have usually united, so simple reduction is no longer possible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. At three months the fracture is long consolidated and would need osteotomy or rhinoplasty rather than reduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A displaced nasal fracture should be reduced to avoid a permanent deformity.

questions.learning_objective: State that a nasal fracture without oedema is reduced early, within about a week.

questions.title: Nasal fracture reduction without oedema (immediate)
questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents 30 minutes after a blow to his face. There is bleeding from the nose and the nose is deviated to the left, with no obvious facial oedema or ecchymosis. X-ray shows a fractured nasal bone. Reduction of this fracture should be performed:

explanations.A: Correct. This patient is seen very early with no oedema to obscure the deformity, so reduction can be carried out immediately. Early reduction before swelling develops gives the most accurate result. When oedema is present instead, reduction is deferred for about a week until it subsides, but that does not apply here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Waiting 24 hours is unnecessary when the patient presents early with no swelling to allow immediate reduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Delaying 48 hours offers no advantage when there is no oedema and immediate reduction is possible.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A week's delay is the plan for a fracture masked by oedema, not for this oedema-free early presentation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. At three months the fracture is consolidated and cannot be simply reduced.

questions.learning_objective: State that an oedema-free nasal fracture seen early can be reduced immediately.

questions.title: Refractory unilateral nasal discharge in a child
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought with a right-sided offensive nasal discharge of two weeks' duration. Several courses of antibiotics and anti-allergic medications have failed. The most probable diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unilateral choanal atresia usually presents with unilateral obstruction rather than a foul discharge unresponsive to treatment.
explanations.B: Correct. A unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a young child that does not respond to antibiotics or anti-allergic treatment is a retained (neglected) nasal foreign body until proven otherwise. The object maintains a foul unilateral discharge no medication can clear. Examination and removal are needed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A deviated septum causes obstruction, not a persistent offensive unilateral discharge in a toddler.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous disease of older patients, not a cause of acute foul discharge in a 3-year-old.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Angiofibroma occurs in adolescent males and presents with obstruction and epistaxis, not a foul toddler discharge.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a treatment-resistant unilateral offensive nasal discharge in a child as a neglected foreign body.

questions.title: Blood-tinged unilateral rhinorrhoea in a child
questions.question: Unilateral offensive blood-tinged purulent rhinorrhoea in a 3-year-old is most likely due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granuloma of older patients, not a cause of acute unilateral discharge in a toddler.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lupus (lupus vulgaris or SLE) is not the usual cause of a foul unilateral discharge at this age.
explanations.C: Correct. A unilateral, offensive, blood-tinged purulent discharge in a young child indicates a retained nasal foreign body. The object causes local ulceration and granulation, which adds blood-staining to the foul discharge. The finding warrants nasal examination and removal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrophic rhinitis is typically bilateral with crusting and cacosmia, and is uncommon at 3 years.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise unilateral blood-tinged offensive rhinorrhoea in a child as a nasal foreign body.

questions.title: True statements about CSF rhinorrhoea
questions.question: All of the following are true about cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea EXCEPT:

options.A: Clear fluid drips from the nose
options.B: Initial treatment is to pack the nose
options.D: The fluid has a salty taste

explanations.A: Incorrect (the statement is true). CSF rhinorrhoea is a clear watery fluid that drips from the nose, typically on one side and increasing on bending forward.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the answer. The nose must NOT be packed in CSF rhinorrhoea, because packing raises the risk of forcing organisms up the leak and producing meningitis. Management is bed rest, head elevation, avoidance of straining and antibiotic cover, with later repair — not nasal packing.
explanations.C: Incorrect (the statement is true). CSF contains glucose, which is one of the bedside/biochemical clues distinguishing it from ordinary nasal mucus.
explanations.D: Incorrect (the statement is true). Patients often notice a salty taste as the CSF trickles into the pharynx.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nose must not be packed in CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.title: Commonest cause of oroantral fistula
questions.question: The most common cause of oroantral fistula is:

options.C: Dental extraction of an upper posterior tooth

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute sinusitis inflames the antral lining but does not by itself create a communication between the mouth and the antrum.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Facial trauma from a road accident is a rare cause compared with dental extraction.
explanations.C: Correct. The commonest cause of an oroantral fistula is extraction of an upper posterior tooth whose roots project into the floor of the maxillary sinus, so their removal opens a communication between the mouth and the antrum. Acute sinusitis, trauma and antral surgery are far less frequent causes. The close relation of the upper premolar and molar roots to the antral floor makes dental extraction the usual culprit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A radical antrum (Caldwell-Luc) operation can occasionally cause a fistula but is much rarer than dental extraction.

questions.learning_objective: State that dental extraction of an upper posterior tooth is the commonest cause of oroantral fistula.

questions.title: Watery nasal discharge that reduces Fehling's solution
questions.question: A unilateral clear watery nasal discharge that reduces Fehling's solution is suggestive of:

explanations.A: Correct. Reduction of Fehling's solution shows that the fluid contains glucose, and a clear watery nasal discharge rich in glucose is cerebrospinal fluid. CSF rhinorrhoea is typically unilateral and increases on bending forward, matching the description. Ordinary nasal mucus does not contain the glucose that reduces Fehling's reagent.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis gives a bilateral watery discharge with sneezing and contains no glucose.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viral rhinitis produces a self-limiting mucoid discharge without glucose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nasal diphtheria causes a blood-stained membranous discharge, not a clear glucose-containing fluid.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a glucose-containing (Fehling-reducing) watery nasal discharge as CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.title: Tooth whose extraction causes oroantral fistula
questions.question: Oroantral fistula commonly follows extraction of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The upper first premolar root is less intimately related to the antral floor than the molar roots.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper canine is anterior and its long root is not related to the maxillary antrum.
explanations.C: Correct. The roots of the upper first molar lie closest to, and often project into, the floor of the maxillary sinus, so extracting it most commonly opens an oroantral communication. The neighbouring premolar and molar roots are related to the antrum as well, but the first molar is the usual offender. This close root-to-antrum relation is the anatomical basis of the fistula.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The upper wisdom tooth is related to the antrum but is a less common cause than the first molar.

questions.learning_objective: State that oroantral fistula most commonly follows extraction of the upper first molar.

questions.title: Character of CSF rhinorrhoea
questions.question: Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea is:

explanations.A: Correct. CSF rhinorrhoea is characteristically a unilateral, clear, watery discharge that leaks from a single skull-base defect. It tastes salty rather than sweet and is colourless, not yellow. Its unilateral, clear nature helps distinguish it from ordinary nasal discharge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. CSF tastes salty, not sweet, even though it contains glucose.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The leak is usually from one skull-base defect, so the discharge is unilateral, not bilateral.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CSF is clear and colourless, not yellowish.

questions.learning_objective: State that CSF rhinorrhoea is a unilateral clear watery discharge.

questions.title: Next step in post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea
questions.question: A young adult male sustains facial trauma in a motor vehicle accident and still has copious clear watery discharge from his nose 24 hours later. The next step is:

options.A: Blowing the nose to clean the nasal cavity

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blowing or straining raises intracranial pressure and can force organisms through the leak, so it is avoided.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nose must not be packed in CSF rhinorrhoea, as packing risks driving infection intracranially.
explanations.C: Correct. Persistent clear watery nasal discharge after a head injury is post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea. Most traumatic leaks close spontaneously, so initial management is conservative: bed rest with the head elevated, avoidance of straining and nose-blowing, and antibiotic cover against meningitis. Nasal packing is contraindicated, and surgical repair is reserved for leaks that do not settle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The head should be elevated, not lowered, to reduce the leak.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that post-traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea is first managed by bed rest and antibiotics, not packing.

questions.title: Criteria of CSF rhinorrhoea except
questions.question: The following are criteria of CSF rhinorrhoea EXCEPT:

options.D: The fluid is rich in glucose

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true feature). CSF rhinorrhoea is a clear watery discharge.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true feature). The leak increases on bending forward as intracranial pressure rises.
explanations.C: Correct. CSF rhinorrhoea is characteristically unilateral, coming from a single skull-base defect, so a commonly bilateral discharge is the exception. The other statements — watery fluid, exacerbation on bending forward and a glucose-rich fluid — are all genuine criteria. Its unilateral, glucose-containing nature is what identifies the leak.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a true feature). CSF contains glucose, unlike ordinary nasal mucus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that a bilateral discharge is not a criterion of CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.title: Features of inverted papilloma
questions.question: In inverted papilloma:

options.B: There is an incidence of malignant transformation
options.C: The treatment is wide local surgical excision

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement itself is true). Inverted papilloma does recur after incomplete removal, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement itself is true). It carries a risk of malignant transformation, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement itself is true). Wide local excision is the correct treatment, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.D: Correct. Inverted (Schneiderian) papilloma of the lateral nasal wall characteristically recurs after incomplete removal, carries a small risk of malignant transformation to squamous carcinoma, and is therefore treated by wide local surgical excision. All three statements are true, so the answer is all of the above. Simple polypectomy is inadequate because it leaves tumour behind.

questions.learning_objective: State that inverted papilloma recurs, may become malignant and needs wide excision.

questions.title: True statement about inverted papilloma
questions.question: "Inverted papilloma" of the nose:

options.B: Arises from the nasal septum in most cases
options.C: Is best diagnosed by carotid angiography
options.D: Should be treated by wide surgical resection to avoid recurrence
options.E: Surgery should be followed by radiation therapy to avoid recurrence

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inverted papilloma is a benign but locally aggressive tumour, though it can transform to malignancy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It arises from the lateral nasal wall, not the septum, in most cases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is diagnosed by endoscopy, imaging and biopsy; carotid angiography is used for vascular tumours such as angiofibroma.
explanations.D: Correct. Inverted papilloma recurs readily if incompletely removed, so it must be treated by wide surgical resection that removes its site of origin on the lateral nasal wall. Adequate excision, rather than simple polypectomy, is what prevents recurrence. It is benign, arises from the lateral wall, and does not need routine post-operative radiotherapy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Routine post-operative radiotherapy is not required; complete surgical excision is the key to avoiding recurrence.

questions.learning_objective: State that inverted papilloma is treated by wide surgical resection to avoid recurrence.

questions.title: Spread of a nasal vestibule furuncle
questions.question: A furuncle of the nasal vestibule should not be squeezed to avoid spread of infection to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Although orbital spread is possible, the classical feared route is intracranial venous spread to the cavernous sinus.
explanations.B: Correct. The nasal vestibule lies in the dangerous area of the face, drained by valveless facial and ophthalmic veins that communicate with the cavernous sinus. Squeezing a furuncle can push infected thrombus along these valveless veins to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis. This is why such furuncles must never be squeezed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sigmoid (lateral) sinus is related to spread from ear and mastoid infection, not from a nasal vestibule furuncle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is a definite danger — spread to the cavernous sinus — so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.subtopic: Nasal vestibule furuncle and the dangerous area of the face
questions.learning_objective: State that a nasal vestibule furuncle can spread to the cavernous sinus.

questions.title: Features of atrophic rhinitis
questions.question: Atrophic rhinitis is characterised by:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). A foul smell (ozaena) is present, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Anosmia is present, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Crust formation is present, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.D: Correct. Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) produces a roomy nose filled with foul greenish crusts, a bad smell noticed by others, and anosmia. Because all three features occur together, the answer is all of the above. The patient is usually anosmic and so does not perceive the foul smell that others notice.

questions.learning_objective: List foul smell, anosmia and crusting as the features of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.title: Atrophic stage of rhinoscleroma
questions.question: In the atrophic stage of rhinoscleroma:

options.A: The middle and inferior turbinates are markedly swollen
options.B: Excessive watery nasal discharge is seen
options.C: The patient has nasal itching and excessive sneezing
options.E: The nose is roomy with considerable crusts

explanations.A: Incorrect. Markedly swollen turbinates are not a feature of the atrophic stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Excessive watery discharge suggests allergic rhinitis, not the atrophic stage of rhinoscleroma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Itching and sneezing are features of allergic rhinitis, not this disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilateral nasal masses belong to the granulomatous (nodular) stage, not the atrophic stage.
explanations.E: Correct. Rhinoscleroma passes through an atrophic (catarrhal), a granulomatous (nodular) and a cicatricial (stenotic) stage. In the atrophic stage the mucosa atrophies so the nose becomes roomy with abundant foul crusts, resembling atrophic rhinitis. Nodular masses and scarring appear only in the later stages.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a roomy crusted nose as the atrophic stage of rhinoscleroma.

questions.title: Infection of the dangerous area of the face
questions.question: Infections in the dangerous area of the face include:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute otitis media is a middle-ear infection, not a dangerous-area-of-the-face infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An infected preauricular cyst lies in front of the ear, outside the dangerous area of the face.
explanations.C: Correct. The dangerous area of the face is the region drained by the valveless facial and ophthalmic veins that communicate with the cavernous sinus. Furunculosis of the nasal vestibule lies within this area, so its infection can spread intracranially to cause cavernous sinus thrombosis. Ear infections drain elsewhere and are not part of this area.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic suppurative otitis media is an ear disease and its complications are otogenic, not facial-venous.

questions.subtopic: Nasal vestibule furuncle and the dangerous area of the face
questions.learning_objective: Identify nasal vestibule furunculosis as an infection of the dangerous area of the face.

questions.hold: Exact in-source duplicate of Q29 (same stem 'In the atrophic stage of rhinoscleroma', same five options a-e, same printed key e); held so the same item is not authored twice.

Non-unique positive stem. 'In atrophic rhinitis' with printed key c (anosmia), but options a (roomy patent nose) and b (bad odour in the nose) are equally true features of atrophic rhinitis, so more than one option is correct; held per the never-guess rule.

Key/stem conflict. 'Scleroma can affect the following sites EXCEPT' with printed key c (bronchi), but scleroma is a disease of the whole respiratory tract and does involve the bronchi, so bronchi cannot be the exception (the least-typical listed site is the lacrimal system); held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Nature of rhinoscleroma
questions.question: Rhinoscleroma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is not a neoplasm; it is an inflammatory granuloma.
explanations.B: Correct. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic specific granuloma of the nose and upper respiratory tract caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis. It is an infective granulomatous disease, not a tumour. Being organism-driven, it is a specific granuloma rather than a chronic non-specific inflammation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is not malignant, although long-standing disease causes scarring and stenosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is a specific (Klebsiella) granuloma, not a non-specific inflammation.

questions.learning_objective: Classify rhinoscleroma as a chronic granuloma of the nose.

questions.hold: Ambiguous / non-unique. 'Choose the false statement regarding atrophic rhinitis' with printed key a (cacosmia); cacosmia is listed elsewhere in this same bank (Q73) as characteristic of atrophic rhinitis, and option c ('nasal granuloma has no role') is also arguably false since granulomatous disease can cause secondary atrophic rhinitis, giving two defensible 'false' statements; held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Pathognomonic cell of rhinoscleroma
questions.question: The pathognomonic cell of rhinoscleroma is the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lymphocytes are non-specific inflammatory cells found in many conditions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plasma cells (and Russell bodies) are seen but are not the pathognomonic cell.
explanations.C: Correct. The Mikulicz cell — a large foamy macrophage containing the causative Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis — is the pathognomonic histological feature of rhinoscleroma. It is accompanied by Russell bodies and plasma cells. Its presence confirms the diagnosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Langhans giant cells are characteristic of tuberculosis, not rhinoscleroma.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the Mikulicz cell as pathognomonic of rhinoscleroma.

questions.hold: Scleroma-site key not cross-checkable. 'Scleroma commonly affects the following sites except' with printed key a (epiglottis); the bank's scleroma-site keys are internally inconsistent (see held Q33), so the intended affected-site list cannot be verified against the options; held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Histopathology of scleroma except
questions.question: The following cells are found in the histopathology of scleroma EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (fibroblasts are present). Fibroblasts appear, especially in the later scarring stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect (Mikulicz cells are present). The Mikulicz cell is the pathognomonic cell of scleroma.
explanations.C: Correct. The histology of scleroma shows Mikulicz cells, Russell bodies, plasma cells and fibroblasts. Langhans giant cells are a feature of tuberculous granuloma, not scleroma, so they are the exception. Their presence should instead suggest tuberculosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect (Russell bodies are present). Russell bodies are immunoglobulin-laden plasma cells characteristic of scleroma.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that Langhans giant cells are not found in scleroma.

questions.hold: Exact in-source duplicate of Q30 (same stem 'Infections in the dangerous area of the face include', same four options, same printed key c); held so the same item is not authored twice.

questions.title: Investigation of an orbital complication of sinusitis
questions.question: A 10-year-old girl presents to the emergency room with a swollen left eyelid. Her illness began a week earlier with fever, nasal discharge and facial pain, progressing to pain around the left eye and oedema of both eyelids. The most informative investigation is:

options.A: Culture and sensitivity of her nasal discharge
options.D: CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nasal culture identifies an organism but does not show the orbital spread or its source.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Serum IgE relates to allergy, not to an orbital complication of sinusitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A complete blood count is supportive only and does not localise the disease.
explanations.D: Correct. The picture is an orbital complication (orbital cellulitis) of acute sinusitis. A CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses is the most informative investigation, showing the diseased sinus, spread through the lamina papyracea and any subperiosteal or orbital abscess. It guides both medical and surgical management.

questions.learning_objective: Select CT of the nose and paranasal sinuses to investigate an orbital complication of sinusitis.

questions.title: Features of allergic fungal sinusitis
questions.question: In allergic fungal sinusitis:

options.B: CT shows heterogeneous soft-tissue opacity and sinus expansion
options.C: Surgery in the form of FESS is the mainstay of treatment

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Specific IgE is elevated, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). CT does show heterogeneous opacity with sinus expansion, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). FESS is the mainstay, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.D: Correct. Allergic fungal sinusitis is a hypersensitivity reaction to fungi in atopic, immunocompetent patients: fungus-specific IgE is elevated, CT shows heterogeneous opacity with expansion of the involved sinus, and functional endoscopic sinus surgery to clear the allergic mucin is the mainstay of treatment. Because all three statements are true, the answer is all of the above. Post-operative steroids help prevent recurrence.

questions.learning_objective: List the immunological, radiological and surgical features of allergic fungal sinusitis.

questions.title: Invasive fulminant fungal sinusitis
questions.question: Invasive fulminant fungal sinusitis:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). It occurs in the immunocompromised, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Mucor is the usual organism, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Amphotericin B is used, but the other statements are also true.
explanations.D: Correct. Acute fulminant invasive fungal sinusitis is an aggressive angio-invasive infection of immunocompromised or poorly controlled diabetic patients, usually caused by Mucor (mucormycosis), and treated with urgent surgical debridement plus systemic amphotericin B. All three statements are true, so the answer is all of the above. Correcting the underlying immune or metabolic state is also essential.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The first three statements are all true, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that invasive fulminant fungal sinusitis is a mucormycosis of the immunocompromised treated with amphotericin B.

questions.title: Presenting signs of acute sinusitis
questions.question: The following is a presenting sign of acute sinusitis:

options.B: Congestion and oedema of the nasal mucosa

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Sinus tenderness is present, but the other signs occur too.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Mucosal congestion is present, but the other signs occur too.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (the statement is true). Mucopurulent discharge is present, but the other signs occur too.
explanations.D: Correct. Acute sinusitis presents with tenderness over the affected sinus, congestion and oedema of the nasal mucosa and a mucopurulent nasal discharge. All three signs are found together, so the answer is all of the above. They accompany facial pain or pressure and nasal obstruction.

questions.learning_objective: List the presenting signs of acute sinusitis.

questions.title: Sinusitis causing orbital cellulitis
questions.question: Orbital cellulitis most commonly occurs after infection of which sinus:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Maxillary sinusitis is a less common source of orbital cellulitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Frontal sinusitis can spread to the orbit but is a less common cause.
explanations.C: Correct. The ethmoid sinuses are separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea, so ethmoid sinusitis is the commonest sinus source of orbital cellulitis. Infection readily crosses this thin plate into the orbit. This is especially true in children.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sphenoid sinusitis is an uncommon cause of orbital cellulitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that ethmoid sinusitis is the commonest sinus source of orbital cellulitis.

questions.hold: Near-exact in-source duplicate of Q40 (identical 10-year-old orbital-cellulitis vignette, same keyed answer CT scan of the nose and paranasal sinuses; only the distractors differ); held so the same item is not authored twice.

questions.title: Orbital complications of sinusitis except
questions.question: Orbital complications of sinusitis include all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is an orbital complication). Orbital cellulitis is the commonest orbital complication of sinusitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is an orbital complication). An orbital or subperiosteal abscess can follow sinusitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is an orbital complication). Cavernous sinus thrombosis is the most serious orbital/intracranial complication.
explanations.D: Correct. Lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis is an otogenic complication of ear and mastoid disease, not an orbital complication of sinusitis. Orbital cellulitis, orbital abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis are the orbital complications of sinusitis. The lateral sinus is therefore the exception.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that lateral sinus thrombosis is otogenic, not an orbital complication of sinusitis.

questions.title: Commonest complication of childhood ethmoid sinusitis
questions.question: The most common complication associated with acute ethmoid sinusitis in children is:

explanations.A: Correct. Acute ethmoid sinusitis is the commonest cause of orbital cellulitis in children, because the ethmoid sinus is separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea. Infection crosses this thin plate to produce orbital cellulitis. Frontal osteomyelitis, subdural abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis are far less common.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Frontal bone osteomyelitis follows frontal sinusitis and is uncommon in young children whose frontal sinus is undeveloped.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A subdural abscess is a rare intracranial complication, not the commonest one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a rare and late complication.

questions.learning_objective: State that orbital cellulitis is the commonest complication of childhood ethmoid sinusitis.

questions.title: Commonest cause of fulminant invasive fungal sinusitis
questions.question: The commonest cause of acute fulminant invasive fungal sinusitis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aspergillus causes chronic and allergic fungal sinusitis more than the acute fulminant form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhinosporidiosis causes a friable nasal polypoidal mass, not fulminant invasive sinusitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Candida is an uncommon cause of fulminant invasive sinusitis.
explanations.D: Correct. Acute fulminant invasive fungal sinusitis is most commonly caused by the Mucorales (mucormycosis), typically in immunocompromised or poorly controlled diabetic patients. The fungus is angio-invasive, causing tissue necrosis, and needs urgent debridement and amphotericin B. Mucor, not Aspergillus, is the classic organism of the fulminant form.

questions.learning_objective: State that mucormycosis is the commonest cause of acute fulminant invasive fungal sinusitis.

questions.title: Most helpful investigation for the nose and paranasal sinuses
questions.question: The most helpful investigation for the nose and the paranasal sinuses is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A plain X-ray gives only a crude view and underestimates both mucosal disease and bony detail.
explanations.B: Correct. CT (usually coronal) is the imaging investigation of choice for the nose and paranasal sinuses. It best demonstrates the bony anatomy, the ostiomeatal complex, the extent of mucosal disease and any bony erosion. This is why it is preferred over plain X-ray, MRI or MRA for most sinonasal problems.
explanations.C: Incorrect. MRI is complementary for soft-tissue characterisation and intracranial extension but is not the first-line sinus investigation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MRA images blood vessels and is used for vascular lesions, not for routine assessment of the sinuses.

questions.learning_objective: State that CT is the most helpful investigation for the nose and paranasal sinuses.

questions.title: Sinus lesion causing lateral displacement of the eyeball
questions.question: Lateral displacement of the eyeball is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sphenoid sinus lies behind the orbit and its lesions do not characteristically push the eyeball laterally.
explanations.B: Correct. The ethmoid sinuses lie medial to the orbit, separated only by the thin lamina papyracea, so an expanding ethmoidal lesion pushes the eyeball laterally. Lesions of the other sinuses displace the globe in other directions. The direction of proptosis therefore points to the sinus involved.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A maxillary sinus lesion, lying below the orbit, tends to displace the eyeball upward, not laterally.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A frontal sinus lesion, lying above and medial, tends to displace the eyeball downward and laterally rather than purely laterally.

questions.learning_objective: State that an ethmoidal sinus lesion displaces the eyeball laterally.

questions.title: Deviated nasal septum facts (except) — FESS
questions.question: The following facts regarding "deviated nasal septum" are true EXCEPT:

options.A: It may be caused by an old trauma
options.B: A sharp septal deviation may be a cause of nasal bleeding
options.C: The treatment of choice is septoplasty
options.D: The treatment is functional endoscopic sinus surgery

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). A deviated septum may follow old nasal trauma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). A sharp septal deviation (spur) can erode the mucosa and cause epistaxis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). Septoplasty (or submucous resection) is the treatment of choice.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement, so it is the answer. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery treats sinus and ostiomeatal disease, not septal deviation; the operation for a deviated septum is septoplasty. FESS therefore has no role in correcting the deviation itself.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that FESS is not the treatment of a deviated nasal septum.

questions.hold: In-source near-duplicate of Q51. Same stem ("deviated nasal septum ... EXCEPT") keying the identical false statement "the treatment is functional endoscopic sinus surgery" (Q51 key d, Q52 key e); Q52 merely adds two true distractors (compensatory contralateral inferior-turbinate hypertrophy, and septoplasty as treatment of choice). Held so the same keyed fact is not authored twice.

questions.title: Deviated nasal septum facts (except) — surgery not contraindicated
questions.question: The following facts regarding "deviated nasal septum" are true EXCEPT:

options.A: It may be caused by an old trauma
options.B: A sharp septal deviation may be a cause of nasal bleeding
options.C: Hypertrophy of the inferior turbinate on the other side of the deviation
options.D: The treatment of choice is septoplasty
options.E: Surgery is contraindicated to avoid septal perforation

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). A deviated septum may follow old trauma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). A sharp deviation can be a source of nasal bleeding.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). Compensatory hypertrophy of the inferior turbinate develops on the wider, concave side opposite the deviation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true). Septoplasty is the treatment of choice.
explanations.E: Correct. This is the false statement. Surgery (septoplasty) is indicated and is not contraindicated; a properly performed submucous septoplasty preserves the mucoperichondrial flaps and does not routinely cause septal perforation. Withholding surgery for fear of perforation is therefore wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that septal surgery is indicated, not contraindicated, in a deviated nasal septum.

questions.title: Septal haematoma — false statement
questions.question: What is not true about septal hematoma:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true). An undrained haematoma strips the cartilage of its blood supply and can cause cartilage necrosis with a saddle-nose deformity.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the false statement. A septal haematoma is a collection of blood that must be drained surgically; decongestants and antihistamines do not treat it. Relying on medical treatment alone risks cartilage necrosis and abscess formation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). It requires surgical incision and drainage.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true). A retained haematoma can become secondarily infected to form a septal abscess.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a septal haematoma is drained surgically, not treated by decongestants and antihistamines.

questions.title: Septal perforation aetiology (except)
questions.question: Septal perforation aetiology can be all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a cause). Habitual nose-picking is a well-recognised cause of anterior septal perforation.
explanations.B: Correct. A congenital deformity of the septum is not a cause of septal perforation; it deviates or malforms the septum but does not create a hole. The genuine causes are trauma, nose-picking, septal abscess, surgery and specific infections or granulomas. Congenital deformity is therefore the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a cause). A septal abscess can necrose the cartilage and leave a perforation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a cause). Septal surgery can perforate the septum.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that congenital deformity is not a cause of nasal septal perforation.

questions.title: Feature of septal haematoma
questions.question: In hematoma of the nasal septum:

options.B: Excessive watery nasal discharge is reported
options.C: The patient smells a bad odour
options.E: The nose is roomy with considerable crusts

explanations.A: Incorrect. A haematoma is a contained collection of blood, not a source of recurrent active epistaxis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Excessive watery discharge suggests allergic rhinitis or CSF rhinorrhoea, not a septal haematoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A bad odour points to atrophic rhinitis or infection, not to an uninfected haematoma.
explanations.D: Correct. A septal haematoma collects on both sides of the septum, producing a boggy bilateral swelling that causes bilateral nasal obstruction. This bilateral block after trauma is the characteristic finding. It must be drained before the cartilage necroses.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A roomy nose with crusts describes atrophic rhinitis, not a septal haematoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that a septal haematoma causes bilateral nasal obstruction.

questions.title: Causes of septal perforation (all of the above)
questions.question: Perforation of the nasal septum may be due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a cause). Trauma, including surgery and nose-picking, perforates the septum, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a cause). A septal abscess necroses the cartilage, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a cause). A nasal granuloma (for example syphilis or a midline granuloma) can perforate the septum, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.D: Correct. Trauma, a septal abscess and a nasal granuloma are all genuine causes of septal perforation, so the answer is all of the above. Each destroys the septal cartilage or its blood supply. Recognising the cause guides management.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since all three listed items are real causes, "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: List trauma, septal abscess and nasal granuloma as causes of septal perforation.

questions.title: Causes of septal perforation (except rhinoscleroma)
questions.question: Causes of nasal septal perforation include all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a cause). Trauma, including surgery, perforates the septum.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a cause). Cocaine sniffing causes ischaemic necrosis of the septal cartilage and perforation.
explanations.C: Correct. Rhinoscleroma characteristically causes scarring and stenosis of the nose rather than a septal perforation, so it is the exception. The typical granulomatous causes of perforation are syphilis and lethal midline granuloma, alongside trauma and cocaine. Rhinoscleroma is therefore the odd one out.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a cause). Syphilis (a gumma) destroys the bony septum and perforates it.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is a cause). Lethal midline (T-cell) granuloma is a destructive midline lesion that perforates the septum.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that rhinoscleroma is not a typical cause of nasal septal perforation.

questions.title: Sneezing as a symptom
questions.question: Sneezing is a common symptom in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sinusitis presents with facial pain, obstruction and mucopurulent discharge rather than paroxysmal sneezing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nasal fracture presents with deformity, bleeding and obstruction, not sneezing.
explanations.C: Correct. Sneezing is a hallmark symptom of allergic rhinitis, an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity of the nasal mucosa. It occurs in paroxysms together with watery rhinorrhoea, itching and obstruction. Sinusitis, nasal fracture and CSF rhinorrhoea do not cause these sneezing attacks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CSF rhinorrhoea is a clear watery leak worse on bending forward; it does not cause sneezing.

questions.learning_objective: State that sneezing is a common symptom of allergic rhinitis.

questions.title: Sneezing, watery discharge and alternating obstruction
questions.question: Attack of sneezing, watery nasal discharge and alternating nasal obstruction can be caused by:

explanations.A: Correct. Paroxysmal sneezing, a watery nasal discharge and nasal obstruction that alternates between the two sides is the classic picture of allergic rhinitis. It is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity, and a nasal smear shows eosinophils. The alternating obstruction reflects the normal nasal cycle exaggerated by mucosal swelling.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granuloma causing masses, crusting or stenosis, not sneezing attacks with watery discharge.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A nasal foreign body causes a unilateral offensive discharge, not bilateral sneezing and watery rhinorrhoea.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CSF rhinorrhoea is a clear watery leak worse on bending forward, without sneezing or alternating obstruction.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise sneezing with watery discharge and alternating obstruction as allergic rhinitis.

questions.title: True statement about antrochoanal polyp
questions.question: Regarding antrochoanal polyp, which is the true statement?

options.A: It usually indicates an underlying fungal infection
options.B: It arises primarily from the ethmoidal sinus
options.C: The primary treatment is endoscopic sinus surgery
options.D: It is precancerous if left untreated
options.E: Observation only is required, since it resolves spontaneously

explanations.A: Incorrect. An antrochoanal polyp is an inflammatory polyp of the maxillary antrum, not a marker of fungal infection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It arises from the maxillary sinus, not the ethmoid.
explanations.C: Correct. The primary treatment of an antrochoanal polyp is endoscopic sinus surgery to remove the polyp together with its origin in the maxillary antrum, which prevents recurrence. Simple avulsion that leaves the antral origin behind tends to recur. It is benign, arises from the maxillary sinus and does not resolve on its own.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is benign and not precancerous.
explanations.E: Incorrect. It does not resolve spontaneously; it needs surgical removal.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primary treatment of an antrochoanal polyp is endoscopic sinus surgery.

questions.title: Correct statement about antrochoanal polyp
questions.question: The following is correct about antrochoanal polyp:

explanations.A: Correct. An antrochoanal polyp is a solitary polyp arising from the maxillary antrum, so it causes unilateral nasal obstruction. It passes through the maxillary ostium and grows back towards the choana, and may reach the nasopharynx. This one-sided obstruction distinguishes it from the bilateral allergic polyps.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It reaches the nose through the maxillary ostium in the middle meatus, not the superior meatus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It is not characteristically associated with a watery discharge; that suggests allergic rhinitis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is removed endoscopically (with or without a radical antrum operation), not usually by lateral rhinotomy.

questions.learning_objective: State that an antrochoanal polyp causes unilateral nasal obstruction.

questions.title: Not characteristic of allergic nasal polypi
questions.question: The following is not characteristic for allergic nasal polypi:

options.C: A nasal smear contains excess eosinophils

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is characteristic). Allergic polyps are multiple and bilateral.
explanations.B: Correct. Allergic nasal polyps arise mainly from the ethmoidal sinuses and middle meatus, not the maxillary sinus, so "arise from the maxillary sinus" is not characteristic. A polyp arising from the maxillary antrum is instead the solitary antrochoanal polyp. This is the option that does not fit allergic polyps.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is characteristic). A nasal smear contains excess eosinophils.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is characteristic). Allergic polyps commonly recur after excision.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that allergic nasal polyps arise from the ethmoid, not the maxillary, sinus.

questions.title: Origin of the antrochoanal polyp
questions.question: Antrochoanal polyp arises from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. It does not arise from the sphenoid sinus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multiple bilateral allergic polyps arise from the ethmoid; the antrochoanal polyp does not.
explanations.C: Incorrect. It does not arise from the frontal sinus.
explanations.D: Correct. An antrochoanal polyp arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum, hence the name "antro-choanal". It passes through the maxillary ostium and grows back towards the choana. Its single maxillary origin distinguishes it from the ethmoidal allergic polyps.

questions.learning_objective: State that the antrochoanal polyp arises from the maxillary sinus.

questions.title: Allergic nasal polypi are bilateral
questions.question: Allergic nasal polypi are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Allergic polyps are not unilateral; a solitary unilateral polyp suggests an antrochoanal polyp.
explanations.B: Correct. Allergic nasal polyps are multiple and bilateral, arising from the ethmoids in atopic patients. They are pale, smooth and mobile, and a nasal smear shows eosinophils. Being bilateral distinguishes them from the solitary antrochoanal polyp.
explanations.C: Incorrect. They are pale and grape-like rather than fleshy; a fleshy single polyp suggests an antrochoanal polyp.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ulceration suggests malignancy, not a benign allergic polyp.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Easy bleeding suggests a vascular tumour such as angiofibroma, not an allergic polyp.

questions.learning_objective: State that allergic nasal polyps are bilateral.

questions.title: Antrochoanal polyp facts (except)
questions.question: In Antrochoanal polyp all is true except:

options.A: Arises usually from the sphenoid sinus
options.D: Is treated by excision with or without radical antrum operation

explanations.A: Correct. This is the false statement. An antrochoanal polyp arises from the maxillary antrum, not the sphenoid sinus, so "arises usually from the sphenoid sinus" is the exception. The maxillary origin is what gives it its name.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true). Being solitary, it causes unilateral nasal obstruction.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true). Its choanal end may extend into the nasopharynx.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true). It is treated by excision with or without a radical antrum operation to remove its origin.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the antrochoanal polyp arises from the maxillary, not sphenoid, sinus.

questions.title: Bilateral nasal obstruction in an adult
questions.question: Bilateral nasal obstruction in a 40 years old adult can be caused by:

explanations.A: Correct. Allergic nasal polyps are multiple and bilateral, so they are the listed cause of bilateral nasal obstruction in an adult. They arise from the ethmoids in atopic patients and block both nasal cavities. The other options cause unilateral obstruction or occur at other ages.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma occurs in adolescent males and causes unilateral obstruction with epistaxis, not bilateral obstruction in a 40-year-old.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bilateral choanal atresia presents in the neonate; unilateral atresia presents later with unilateral obstruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A foreign body is a problem of young children and causes unilateral obstruction.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise bilateral allergic nasal polyps as a cause of bilateral nasal obstruction in an adult.

questions.title: Commonest cause of epistaxis
questions.question: The most common cause of epistaxis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A congenital blood disease is a rare cause of epistaxis compared with idiopathic bleeding.
explanations.B: Correct. The commonest cause of epistaxis is idiopathic (spontaneous) bleeding, typically from the exposed vessels of Little’s area on the anteroinferior septum. It is far more common than local disease such as rhinoscleroma or chronic sinusitis. Most such bleeds are minor and anterior.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is an uncommon local cause of epistaxis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic sinusitis is an uncommon cause of epistaxis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest cause of epistaxis is idiopathic.

questions.title: Commonest cause of epistaxis in the elderly
questions.question: The most common cause of epistaxis in elderly is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A congenital blood disease usually presents earlier in life and is not the common elderly cause.
explanations.B: Correct. In elderly patients the commonest cause of epistaxis is hypertension, which tends to produce a more profuse posterior bleed from the sphenopalatine vessels. Blood pressure should be checked and controlled as part of management. This contrasts with the idiopathic anterior bleeds of children and young adults.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is an uncommon cause and not specific to the elderly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chronic sinusitis is an uncommon cause of epistaxis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A septal perforation may bleed a little but is not the commonest elderly cause.

questions.learning_objective: State that hypertension is the commonest cause of epistaxis in the elderly.

questions.title: Best treatment of mild epistaxis from Little’s area
questions.question: The best treatment of mild epistaxis from Little’s area is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anterior nasal packing is reserved for diffuse or brisk anterior bleeding, not for a discrete visible point.
explanations.B: Correct. When epistaxis is mild and the bleeding point is visible in Little’s area, the best treatment is cautery of that point, using chemical (silver nitrate) or electrocautery after local decongestion and anaesthesia. Directed cautery is definitive for a discrete anterior bleeding point. Packing and transfusion are for heavier bleeding.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A posterior pack is used for posterior epistaxis, not a mild anterior bleed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood transfusion is only needed for significant blood loss, not for mild epistaxis.

questions.learning_objective: State that mild epistaxis from a visible point in Little’s area is treated by cautery.

questions.title: Commonest site of epistaxis
questions.question: The commonest site for epistaxis is:

options.A: The anterior end of the nasal septum
options.B: The posterior end of the nasal septum
options.C: The anterior end of the inferior turbinate
options.D: The posterior end of the inferior turbinate

explanations.A: Correct. The commonest site of epistaxis is the anterior end of the nasal septum, which is Little’s area (Kiesselbach’s plexus) on the anteroinferior septum. Its exposed anastomotic vessels bleed easily from trauma or drying. Most nosebleeds, especially in children, come from here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior septum is the site of the heavier posterior epistaxis of the elderly, not the commonest overall site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anterior end of the inferior turbinate is not the classic bleeding site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior end of the inferior turbinate (Woodruff’s plexus) is an occasional posterior source, not the commonest site.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest site of epistaxis is Little’s area on the anterior septum.

questions.title: Commonest cause of epistaxis in a child
questions.question: The commonest cause for epistaxis in a 5 years old child is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Angiofibroma occurs in adolescent males, not typically a 5-year-old, and is uncommon.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a chronic granuloma of older patients, not the common childhood cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Inverted papilloma is a tumour of adults, not a cause of childhood epistaxis.
explanations.D: Correct. The commonest cause of epistaxis in a young child is idiopathic bleeding from Little’s area, usually precipitated by nose-picking or drying. It is far more common than any tumour or granuloma. Most such bleeds are minor and anterior.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest cause of epistaxis in a child is idiopathic.

questions.hold: Non-unique / key-vs-content tension. "Cacosmia is a characteristic symptom in cases of" with printed key b (sinusitis of dental origin), but two options are defensible: dental (anaerobic) sinusitis gives a foul smell the patient perceives (cacosmia), while atrophic rhinitis (option c) is the classically taught association of cacosmia — and this same bank’s Q35 cross-check treats cacosmia as characteristic of atrophic rhinitis. Two defensible answers (b and c) make it non-unique; held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Cause of unilateral nasal obstruction
questions.question: A cause of unilateral nasal obstruction:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Allergic rhinitis is a bilateral mucosal disease and causes bilateral obstruction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhinoscleroma is a diffuse granulomatous disease that tends to affect the nose bilaterally.
explanations.C: Correct. Cancer of the maxilla (maxillary antrum) is a one-sided lesion, so it causes unilateral nasal obstruction. A persistent unilateral block, especially with blood-stained discharge, must raise the suspicion of a sinonasal neoplasm. The bilateral mucosal diseases in the other options obstruct both sides.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The common cold is an acute viral rhinitis that obstructs both nasal cavities.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise cancer of the maxilla as a cause of unilateral nasal obstruction.

questions.title: Commonest cause of epistaxis in children
questions.question: The commonest cause of epistaxis in children is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenoids cause nasal obstruction and mouth-breathing, not the common childhood nosebleed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nasopharyngeal fibroma (angiofibroma) affects adolescent males and is uncommon.
explanations.C: Correct. The commonest cause of epistaxis in children is idiopathic bleeding from Little’s area, usually precipitated by nose-picking or drying of the mucosa. It is far more common than adenoids, angiofibroma or a foreign body. Such bleeds are typically minor and anterior.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A foreign body causes a unilateral offensive discharge; it is not the commonest cause of epistaxis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the commonest cause of epistaxis in children is idiopathic.

questions.title: Causes of unilateral nasal obstruction (except)
questions.question: Causes of unilateral nasal obstruction includes the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a cause). Unilateral choanal atresia blocks one side.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a cause). An antrochoanal polyp is solitary and obstructs one side.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a cause). Sinusitis of dental origin is a unilateral maxillary sinus disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a cause). A sinonasal neoplasm is a one-sided lesion causing unilateral obstruction.
explanations.E: Correct. Allergic rhinitis is a bilateral mucosal disease and causes bilateral, not unilateral, obstruction, so it is the exception. The other four options are all one-sided lesions. A unilateral block therefore points to a local structural cause rather than allergy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that allergic rhinitis causes bilateral, not unilateral, nasal obstruction.

questions.title: Systemic causes of epistaxis
questions.question: Systemic causes of epistaxis include:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a systemic cause). Hypertension raises vascular pressure and causes bleeding, but the other options are also systemic causes.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a systemic cause). Leukaemia is a blood dyscrasia that impairs haemostasis, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a systemic cause). Anticoagulant drugs promote bleeding, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a systemic cause). Liver cell failure impairs clotting-factor synthesis, but the other options are also causes.
explanations.E: Correct. Hypertension, blood dyscrasias such as leukaemia, anticoagulant drugs and liver cell failure are all systemic causes of epistaxis, so the answer is all of the above. They act by raising vascular pressure or impairing haemostasis. Recognising a systemic cause is essential because local measures alone may not stop the bleeding.

questions.learning_objective: List hypertension, blood dyscrasias, anticoagulants and liver failure as systemic causes of epistaxis.

questions.title: Indications of endoscopic sinus surgery (except)
questions.question: Endoscopic sinus surgery is indicated in the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is an indication). Allergic fungal sinusitis is treated by FESS to clear the allergic mucin.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is an indication). Extensive sinonasal polyposis is a standard indication for FESS.
explanations.C: Correct. Atrophic rhinitis is managed medically with nasal toilet and moisturising, not by endoscopic sinus surgery, so it is the exception. FESS is aimed at restoring sinus ventilation and drainage or removing disease, which atrophic rhinitis does not require. It is therefore the odd one out.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is an indication). An antrochoanal polyp is removed endoscopically.
explanations.E: Incorrect (this is an indication). Inverted papilloma is resected endoscopically in suitable cases.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that atrophic rhinitis is not an indication for endoscopic sinus surgery.

questions.title: Complications of FESS
questions.question: Complications of Functional endoscopic sinus surgery might include:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a complication). Bleeding can occur, but the other complications also occur.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a complication). Nasal adhesions (synechiae) can form, but the other complications also occur.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer (it is a complication). A CSF leak can follow a skull-base breach, but the other complications also occur.
explanations.D: Correct. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery can be complicated by bleeding, nasal adhesions and a CSF leak (and orbital injury), so the answer is all of the above. These reflect the close relation of the sinuses to the orbit and anterior cranial fossa. Careful technique and anatomical knowledge minimise them.

questions.learning_objective: List bleeding, nasal adhesions and CSF leak among the complications of FESS.
